title: Concurrent Collections
subtopics: Choosing collections according to concurrency patterns
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of concurrent collections and identify when it is appropriate in a Java program.
Apply at least one of the lesson topics—concurrenthashmap—in a small, readable example.
Identify one failure, compatibility, security, or resource-management concern and describe a safe response.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study concurrent collections with a short explanation, an original visual map, a Java example, and a check you can perform yourself. Focus on the relationship between the rule and the behavior rather than memorizing isolated syntax.
content.why_it_matters: This concept matters because it helps you coordinate tasks without depending on unpredictable scheduling or shared mutable state. In this lesson, focus on concurrenthashmap and use a minimal example to check what the rule actually guarantees.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Choose a collection according to ordering, uniqueness, lookup, and update requirements. Review equals/hashCode contracts, iteration behavior, and concurrent-modification rules before selecting an implementation. The important habit is to make the assumptions explicit and use the code example as a small experiment.

content_blocks.title: How the pieces fit
content_blocks.text: Connect concurrenthashmap with blocking queues before choosing an implementation. The example is a small, observable case; extend it by changing one input and checking a boundary, invalid value, or compatibility limit where relevant.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming one timing or memory observation proves a performance conclusion.
common_mistakes.why: JIT warm-up, scheduling, allocation, and workload changes can distort single measurements.
common_mistakes.fix: Use repeatable workloads and appropriate JDK diagnostics, and record the environment.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing only a single happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Boundary values and failures often reveal assumptions hidden by the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add an empty, boundary, or invalid case and state the expected behavior before running it.

common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify the actual cause of a different result.
common_mistakes.fix: Change one factor at a time and keep a short record of observed behavior.
